stem: Which pair of monosaccharides forms sucrose?

options.rationale: Correct: sucrose is α-glucose joined to fructose.
Two α-glucose molecules form maltose.
Glucose and galactose form lactose.
These do not combine to form any of the three common disaccharides.

explanation: Maltose = glucose + glucose; sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose.

stem: How does β-glucose differ from α-glucose?

options.content: The –OH group on carbon 1 is above the ring instead of below it
options.rationale: Correct: only the position of the OH on carbon 1 differs.

options.content: It has five carbon atoms in its ring instead of six
options.rationale: Both have a ring of five carbons and one oxygen; both are hexoses with six carbons in total.

options.content: The –CH₂OH group on carbon 5 is below the ring instead of above it
options.rationale: Carbon 6 (the CH₂OH) is above the ring in both forms.

options.content: It has the formula C₆H₁₀O₅ instead of C₆H₁₂O₆
options.rationale: Both have the same formula, C₆H₁₂O₆; they are isomers.

explanation: α- and β-glucose are isomers: same formula, OH on carbon 1 below (α) or above (β) the plane of the ring.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the formation of a glycosidic bond?

options.content: A hydrolysis reaction in which a single molecule of water is removed
options.rationale: Hydrolysis adds water and breaks bonds.

options.content: A condensation reaction in which a molecule of water is added
options.rationale: Condensation releases water; it does not add it.

options.content: A hydrolysis reaction in which a molecule of water is added
options.rationale: This describes breaking a glycosidic bond, not forming one.

options.content: A condensation reaction in which a molecule of water is removed
options.rationale: Correct: two –OH groups react; H₂O is released and C–O–C links the sugars.

explanation: Condensation: bond formed, water removed. Hydrolysis: water added, bond broken.

stem: Which sugar is a pentose?

options.rationale: Glucose is a hexose (six carbons).
Correct: ribose has five carbon atoms (C₅H₁₀O₅).
Fructose is a hexose (six carbons).
Maltose is a disaccharide with twelve carbons.

explanation: Pentoses (5C): ribose and deoxyribose, found in RNA and DNA. Hexoses (6C): glucose, fructose, galactose.

stem: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar?

options.content: It contains fructose, and fructose on its own is not a reducing sugar at all
options.rationale: Fructose on its own is a reducing sugar.

options.content: Its glycosidic bond uses the reactive groups of both glucose and fructose
options.rationale: Correct: carbon 1 of glucose bonds to carbon 2 of fructose, so no free reducing group remains.

options.content: It is too large a molecule to react with copper(II) ions
options.rationale: Maltose and lactose are the same size and are reducing sugars.

options.content: It is insoluble in water, so it cannot mix with Benedict's
options.rationale: Sucrose is very soluble in water.

explanation: In maltose and lactose one unit keeps a free carbon 1, so they reduce Benedict's. In sucrose both reactive carbons are in the bond. Acid hydrolysis frees them.
hints: Which carbons are used to make the bond in sucrose?

stem: A chain of 12 glucose molecules is formed by condensation. How many molecules of water are released?

options.rationale: This assumes one water per glucose; the end units each make only one bond.
This counts two waters per glucose; each bond releases only one.
Correct: a chain of n units has n − 1 bonds, and each bond releases one water molecule.
This would be the number of disaccharide pairs, not the number of bonds in a single chain.

explanation: Twelve units in a single unbranched chain are joined by 11 glycosidic bonds, so 11 molecules of water are released (and 11 would be needed to hydrolyse it completely).
hints: Count the bonds, not the units.

stem: A sample of a disaccharide gives a positive Benedict's test. After complete hydrolysis, the products are found to be glucose only. Which disaccharide was it?

options.rationale: Sucrose is non-reducing and hydrolyses to glucose and fructose.
Correct: maltose is reducing and is hydrolysed to two glucose molecules.
Lactose is reducing but hydrolyses to glucose and galactose.
Cellulose is a polysaccharide, not a disaccharide, and does not dissolve to give a positive Benedict's test.

explanation: Reducing + glucose only → maltose. Lactose also gives galactose; sucrose gives fructose and is non-reducing.
hints: Use both pieces of evidence: reducing and the products.

stem: The relative molecular mass of glucose is 180 and that of fructose is also 180. Calculate the relative molecular mass of sucrose formed from them by condensation (water has Mr 18).
explanation: 180 + 180 − 18 = 342. Forgetting to remove water gives 360; adding it gives 378.
workedSolution: 1. 180 + 180 − 18 = 342. Forgetting to remove water gives 360; adding it gives 378.

stem: Calculate the relative molecular mass of an unbranched chain of 40 glucose molecules (glucose Mr = 180; water Mr = 18).
explanation:
1. Mass of 40 glucose units: $40 \times 180 = 7200$.
2. A chain of 40 units has 39 glycosidic bonds, so 39 water molecules are removed: $39 \times 18 = 702$.
3. $M_r = 7200 - 702 = 6498$.
4. Subtracting 40 waters (720) gives 6480; forgetting the water gives 7200.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Mass of 40 glucose units: $40 \times 180 = 7200$.
2. A chain of 40 units has 39 glycosidic bonds, so 39 water molecules are removed: $39 \times 18 = 702$.
3. $M_r = 7200 - 702 = 6498$.
4. Subtracting 40 waters (720) gives 6480; forgetting the water gives 7200.
hints: How many bonds join 40 units in a line?

stem: Raffinose is a trisaccharide made from three hexose units (each Mr 180) joined by condensation. Calculate its relative molecular mass (water Mr 18).
explanation: 3 × 180 = 540; two bonds release 2 × 18 = 36; 540 − 36 = 504. Removing only one water gives 522.
workedSolution: 1. 3 × 180 = 540; two bonds release 2 × 18 = 36; 540 − 36 = 504. Removing only one water gives 522.
hints: Three units in a chain are joined by two bonds.

stem: Lactose is a disaccharide found in milk.
explanation: True. Lactose (glucose + galactose) is the main sugar in milk; it is hydrolysed by the enzyme lactase.

stem: Hydrolysis of a glycosidic bond removes a molecule of water.
explanation: False. Hydrolysis **adds** water to break the bond; condensation removes water to form it.

stem: Match each disaccharide with the monosaccharides that form it.
explanation: Maltose: two glucose; sucrose: glucose + fructose; lactose: glucose + galactose.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: In maltose the two glucose units are joined by an {{blank:a}} glycosidic bond between carbon 1 of one glucose and carbon {{blank:b}} of the other. The enzyme that hydrolyses maltose is {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Maltose has an α-1,4 glycosidic bond, hydrolysed by maltase. Amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose.

stem: Give the name of the bond that joins two monosaccharides.
explanation: A **glycosidic bond** (C–O–C) is formed by condensation between two sugars.

stem: Give the general formula of a monosaccharide.
explanation: Monosaccharides have the general formula **(CH₂O)ₙ**, with n from 3 to 7. C₆H₁₂O₆ is glucose specifically (n = 6).

stem: Describe how two α-glucose molecules join to form maltose and how maltose is broken down again.

points.description: The –OH on carbon 1 of one α-glucose reacts with the –OH on carbon 4 of the other
Condensation reaction: a molecule of water is removed
Hydrolysis: water is added to break the bond, catalysed by maltase (or by boiling with acid)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The hydroxyl group on carbon 1 of one α-glucose reacts with the hydroxyl group on carbon 4 of a second α-glucose. A molecule of water is removed in this condensation reaction, leaving an α-1,4 glycosidic bond. Maltose is broken down by hydrolysis: a molecule of water is added to the bond, a reaction catalysed by maltase in the small intestine (or by boiling with acid).

explanation: Name the carbons, the reaction type, the water and the bond.
hints: Which carbons take part, and what is lost?

stem: Suggest why sucrose rather than glucose is the main sugar transported in the phloem of plants such as sugar cane.

points.description: Sucrose is non-reducing so it is less reactive / is not used up (metabolised) by cells on the way
Sucrose is still very soluble, so it can be transported in solution in phloem sap
Disaccharide carries twice as many sugar units per molecule, so less osmotic effect for the same energy (or transported energy per solute particle greater)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sucrose is non-reducing, so it is chemically less reactive and is less likely to be used in reactions by the cells it passes on its way. It is highly soluble, so it is easily carried in phloem sap. Each sucrose molecule carries two hexose units, so more sugar is transported for a smaller effect on water potential.

explanation: A *suggest* item: any three valid reasons.
hints: Think about reactivity, solubility and osmotic effect.

stem:
Three unlabelled sugar solutions, X, Y and Z, are each known to be one of maltose, sucrose and lactose. A student carries out tests.

| Solution | Benedict's (heated) | Products after complete hydrolysis |
|---|---|---|
| X | Blue | Glucose and fructose |
| Y | Brick-red | Glucose only |
| Z | Brick-red | Glucose and galactose |

parts.label: (a)
parts.explanation: X: non-reducing, glucose + fructose = sucrose. Y: reducing, glucose only = maltose. Z: reducing, glucose + galactose = lactose.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why X gave a negative result with Benedict's solution, but its hydrolysis products would give a positive result.

points.description: The glycosidic bond in sucrose involves carbon 1 of glucose and carbon 2 of fructose
So there is no free reducing group to reduce copper(II) ions
Hydrolysis breaks the bond and frees the reducing groups of glucose and fructose (both reducing sugars)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In sucrose the glycosidic bond joins carbon 1 of glucose to carbon 2 of fructose, so both reducing groups are used and none can reduce the copper(II) ions in Benedict's solution. Hydrolysis breaks this bond, releasing glucose and fructose, which are both reducing sugars.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe how the student could hydrolyse solution X and show that reducing sugars had been produced.

points.description: Boil X with dilute hydrochloric acid
Cool and neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate
Benedict's test with heating gives brick-red / orange precipitate
Control: an unhydrolysed sample of X (or acid + alkali + water only) tested in the same way stays blue

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Boil a sample of X with dilute hydrochloric acid, cool it, neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate, then add Benedict's solution and heat; a brick-red precipitate shows reducing sugars. A sample of X that was not hydrolysed, tested the same way, stays blue as a control.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The Mr of each monosaccharide is 180 and of water 18. Calculate the Mr of Z.

parts.label: (e)

options.rationale: Maltase hydrolyses maltose.
Sucrase hydrolyses sucrose.
Correct: lactase hydrolyses lactose.
Amylase hydrolyses starch.

parts.explanation: Enzymes are specific: lactase for lactose.

explanation: Combine the reducing property with the hydrolysis products to identify each disaccharide.

stem: A dairy in Mutare makes lactose-reduced milk by adding the enzyme lactase. Rudo tests samples of milk before and after treatment.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which products are formed when lactase acts on lactose?

options.rationale: These are the products of sucrose hydrolysis.
These are the products of maltose hydrolysis.
These are the products of lipid hydrolysis.
Correct: lactose is glucose joined to galactose.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the type of reaction catalysed by lactase.
parts.explanation: Water is added to break the glycosidic bond: hydrolysis.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Both untreated and treated milk give a positive Benedict's test. Explain why.

points.description: Lactose is a reducing sugar (one unit has a free reactive carbon 1)
Glucose and galactose (products) are also reducing sugars

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Lactose is itself a reducing sugar, because one of its units has a free reactive group, and its products, glucose and galactose, are also reducing sugars.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest how a semi-quantitative Benedict's test could show that lactase had acted.

points.description: Treated milk gives a stronger colour / more precipitate / shorter time to colour change under standardised conditions
Because each lactose gives two reducing monosaccharides, so more reducing groups per volume

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Under identical conditions the treated milk would give more precipitate (a colour further towards brick-red) or change colour sooner, because each lactose molecule has become two reducing sugars.

explanation: Lactase hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose; all three are reducing sugars, but hydrolysis increases the number of reducing groups.
